title: Choosing an orchestration
summary: The five built-in orchestrations differ by topology, who decides the next step and how much they cost. Start with the simplest that fits the task shape, and escalate only when evidence says it is needed.
useIf: You have several agents and must pick sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat or Magentic, or decide that an agent-as-tool or custom workflow is better.
avoidIf: A single agent with tools meets quality and latency targets: multi-agent adds cost, context isolation work and failure modes.

explain.md: Topology drives behaviour. **Sequential** is a pipeline. **Concurrent** is fan-out and aggregate. **Handoff** is a mesh with no central orchestrator, where the receiving agent owns the task. **Group chat** is a star with an orchestrator that picks the speaker over a shared full history. **Magentic** is group chat plus a planning manager with a progress ledger. The docs add that Magentic adds planning cost and is untested outside its original design, so start with group chat unless the path truly needs planning [[tr23]] [[tr24]] [[tr25]] [[tr26]] [[tr27]].

**Rules of thumb that come from the mechanics.** Latency: sequential sums, concurrent takes the slowest, group chat and Magentic multiply rounds. Tokens: group chat and handoff re-share history with every participant, so cost grows with rounds and participants, while Magentic adds manager calls on top. Control: only handoff returns to a user by default; approvals in the others arrive as request events. Every built-in orchestration is a workflow underneath, so `as_agent()`, checkpoint storage and human-in-the-loop requests work the same way, and you can drop to a custom graph when the pattern does not fit [[tr14]].

explain.title: A decision order that avoids over-engineering

steps.title: Function or one agent?
steps.md: If code or one agent with tools works, stop.

steps.title: Fixed dependent order?
steps.md: Yes: sequential, or a graph if you need branches and gates.

steps.title: Should ownership move to specialists?
steps.md: Yes: handoff. Primary keeps ownership: agent-as-tool.

steps.title: Unknown path, many rounds?
steps.md: Magentic, with limits and plan review.

blocks.code:
from agent_framework.orchestrations import (SequentialBuilder, ConcurrentBuilder,
    HandoffBuilder, GroupChatBuilder, MagenticBuilder)

seq  = SequentialBuilder(participants=[a, b, c]).build()
conc = ConcurrentBuilder(participants=[a, b, c]).build()
hand = HandoffBuilder(name='h', participants=[a, b, c]).with_start_agent(a).build()
chat = GroupChatBuilder(participants=[a, b], selection_func=pick,
                        termination_condition=done).build()
mag  = MagenticBuilder(participants=[a, b], manager_agent=mgr,
                       max_round_count=10).build()
# all are workflows: .as_agent(), checkpoint_storage=..., HITL work the same way

whereToUse: Design reviews: choosing the topology before writing agents
Cost reviews: spotting patterns whose token cost scales with rounds and participants
Migration from AutoGen teams: mapping Team types to workflow orchestrations
Interviews: justifying why you did not reach for the most capable pattern

use: Task shape is clear: independent, dependent, ownership transfer, iterative or unknown
You can state latency, cost and audit requirements before choosing
You will measure the multi-agent design against a single-agent baseline
avoid: Picking Magentic because it sounds most capable
Multi-agent without evaluation evidence that it beats one agent
Using group chat where a fixed pipeline is enough
flips: Provable order or approvals at specific steps: leave orchestrations and use a custom workflow graph
A primary agent must stay accountable for the final answer: use agent-as-tool instead of handoff

pitfalls.symptom: Costs rise sharply after adding more agents to a group chat
pitfalls.cause: Every turn re-sends the shared history and rounds multiply
pitfalls.fix: Cap rounds, compact, limit participants or move independent work to concurrent

pitfalls.symptom: The team cannot explain why Magentic was chosen
pitfalls.cause: Chosen for capability, not for an unknown path
pitfalls.fix: Write down the task shape and fall back to group chat or a graph if the path is knowable

pitfalls.symptom: An orchestration cannot satisfy an approval requirement
pitfalls.cause: Sequential, concurrent and group chat do not pause for free text
pitfalls.fix: Use handoff, a request port in a custom graph, or tool approvals

scenarios.title: Incident response assistant
scenarios.situation: During an incident the assistant should gather logs, metrics and recent deploys in parallel, then a coordinator reasons over everything and suggests actions. Time to first insight matters: under 30 seconds.
unknowns: Does a coordinator need a debate?
What if one source is down?
scenarios.question: Which pattern?

options.name: Concurrent gatherers with an aggregator, followed by a single coordinator agent (a small custom graph or a sequential step after the aggregator)
options.why: Independent gathers run in parallel, so latency is about the slowest source, and one coordinator reasons over the merged data.
options.tradeoff: Cost is three gatherer runs plus the coordinator; a failed source needs explicit handling.

options.name: Magentic with specialists
options.why: The path is known (gather, then reason), so planning calls only add latency and cost.
options.tradeoff: Right when each incident needs a different investigation path.

options.name: Sequential gatherers
options.tradeoff: Latency is the sum of three slow queries, which may exceed 30 seconds.

flips.then: Add timeouts and partial-result handling in the aggregator.

scenarios.takeaway: When the shape is known, use the pattern that matches it: independent then merge.

scenarios.title: Product Q&A that sometimes needs an expert
scenarios.situation: A product assistant answers most questions alone. Pricing and legal questions should move to a specialist who then continues with the user. Volume is high and cost matters.
unknowns: How often do pricing and legal questions occur?
scenarios.question: How do you wire the agents?

options.name: Handoff: a generalist start agent with pricing and legal specialists it can hand to
options.why: Ownership moves to the specialist who then talks to the user, and most chats never leave the generalist.
options.tradeoff: Mesh broadcast adds some tokens, and routing quality depends on the prompts.

options.name: Agent-as-tool: generalist calls specialists
options.why: Cheaper to reason about and the generalist stays accountable.
options.tradeoff: The generalist relays answers, so specialist voice and follow-ups are filtered.

options.name: Group chat with all agents on every question
options.why: Pays for several agents on every question where most need one.

flips.if: Routing can be decided by a keyword or tier
flips.then: Use a conditional edge instead of an LLM handoff.

scenarios.takeaway: Match the pattern to who should talk to the user.

scenarios.title: Do we need multi-agent at all?
scenarios.situation: A team proposes five agents for a task that fits in one context window. Eval data shows a single agent scores 91 percent. The five-agent prototype scores 93 percent at 4 times the cost.
unknowns: Is the 2 point gain statistically significant?
scenarios.question: What do you recommend?

options.name: Keep the single agent, check significance and error types, and revisit if a category of errors needs role separation
options.why: A 2 point gain for 4 times the cost is rarely worth it, and it may be within noise.
options.tradeoff: You forgo a small possible gain.

options.name: Ship the five-agent design
options.why: Quadruples cost and failure surface for a marginal gain.
options.tradeoff: Right when the gain targets a costly error class.

options.name: Use concurrent voting on all requests
options.why: May raise quality with less design.
options.tradeoff: Still multiplies cost and needs proof.

flips.if: Errors are expensive, such as legal or medical
flips.then: Pay for a reviewer agent on the high-risk class only.

flips.if: Task grows beyond the context window

scenarios.takeaway: Earn each extra agent with measured gains.

quiz.q: Match each orchestration to its topology.
quiz.explain: Magentic has the group chat shape with a planning manager. Handoff agents connect in a mesh because they share context.

quiz.q: A task needs several specialists, the path is not known in advance, and the budget allows planning calls. Which pattern fits, per the docs?
quiz.explain: Magentic targets complex open-ended tasks with dynamic planning. The docs recommend group chat when complex planning is not needed.

quiz.q: Which requirements push you away from the built-in orchestrations toward a custom workflow? Select all.
options: Approval at one specific step that may take days
Three agents reviewing the same draft in parallel
quiz.explain: Parallel independent review is exactly what concurrent orchestration provides.

flashcards.front: Which orchestration returns control to a user by default?
flashcards.back: Handoff. Sequential, concurrent and group chat do not pause for free text on their own.

flashcards.front: Why start with group chat before Magentic?
flashcards.back: Magentic adds planning cost and is untested outside Magentic-One's design, so use it only when the path truly needs planning.

flashcards.front: Which pattern's latency is bounded by the slowest participant?
